1	\section{Related Work}

4	\paragraph{Model Collapse and Recursive Generation.}
5	Training on model-generated data can cause progressive distribution shift known as \emph{model collapse}.
6	Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} showed that iteratively training language models on their own outputs leads to irreversible tail-distribution degradation, with minority modes vanishing across generations.
7	Alemohammad et al.~\cite{alemohammad2024selfconsuming} formalized this for self-consuming generative models, proving convergence to a fixed point under mild regularity conditions.
8	Dohmatob et al.~\cite{dohmatob2024model} derived scaling laws for collapse, demonstrating that tail probability mass is lost at rates predictable from model and data scale.
9	Further work shows that even a vanishingly small fraction of synthetic data suffices to trigger collapse, with the effect amplified in larger models~\citep{dohmatob2025strong}; their distribution-shift analysis and our information-theoretic derivation of $\Kstar$ arrive at the same conclusion from complementary starting points---recursive generation inevitably degrades information to a finite boundary.
10	Schaeffer et al.~\cite{schaeffer2025position} organized the fragmented literature into a taxonomy of eight definitions across three families.
11	Our $\Kstar$ aligns with their Family~B (distributional deformation), specifically D4 (collapsing variance) and D6 (mode entanglement)---the features that degrade most rapidly in our experiments are precisely variance-based surprisal measures.
12	Kazdan et al.~\cite{kazdan2025collapse} distinguished \emph{replace} and \emph{accumulate} regimes: in the replace regime each generation completely supplants its predecessor, producing faster collapse.
13	Our prompt-chain protocol operates in the replace regime, so $\Kempirical = 2$ is a conservative lower bound; the accumulate regime would yield slower degradation and higher $\Kstar$.
14	Shi et al.~\cite{shi2025generalization} identified a generalization-to-memorization transition in recursively trained models, providing cross-modal evidence that information loss is progressive.
15	Gerstgrasser et al.~\cite{gerstgrasser2024inevitable} proved that collapse is avoidable when sufficient original data is retained alongside synthetic samples, a condition that depth-aware curation can enforce by construction.
16	These works characterize the macro dynamics of collapse but do not provide tools for per-text generational depth estimation.
17	
18	\paragraph{Binary Synthetic Text Detection.}
19	Distinguishing machine-generated from human-written text is a well-studied binary classification problem.
20	Early statistical approaches such as GLTR~\cite{gehrmann2019gltr} visualized per-token likelihood ranks to help human annotators spot generated text, establishing that token-level distributional cues are informative for detection.
21	Zellers et al.~\cite{zellers2019grover} demonstrated that the generating model itself is an effective detector, while Ippolito et al.~\cite{ippolito2020detection} analyzed how detection difficulty scales with generation quality.
22	Recent zero-shot methods have narrowed the gap: Mitchell et al.~\cite{mitchell2023detectgpt} introduced DetectGPT, which uses probability curvature to detect machine-generated text without access to the generating model.
23	Fast-DetectGPT~\citep{bao2024fast} dramatically accelerates this approach via conditional probability curvature, achieving a 340$\times$ speedup with improved accuracy.
24	Hans et al.~\cite{hans2024binoculars} proposed Binoculars, which computes the cross-perplexity ratio between two closely related language models to achieve near-perfect detection without any training data.
25	DivEye~\cite{basani2026diveye} uses surprisal diversity features to detect synthetic text without generator-specific training data; their surprisal diversity features overlap with the \texttt{surp\_*} subset of our 15-dimensional feature set, but DivEye optimizes for binary detection whereas our features target ordinal depth discrimination---the same feature family serving tasks at different granularities.
26	Min-K\%++~\cite{zhang2024minkpp} adapts membership inference techniques to flag model-generated passages via outlier token likelihoods.
27	CoDeC~\cite{zawalski2026codec} frames contamination detection as in-context learning, calibrating thresholds from few-shot exemplars.
28	
29	All these methods produce binary outputs and do not distinguish generational depth.
30	The connection to membership inference is instructive: Min-K\%++ and related approaches test whether a text appeared in training data---a related but distinct question from how many recursive generation steps it has undergone.
31	A further limitation is that binary detectors cannot separate beneficial recursive generation (e.g., self-refinement, where a model iteratively improves its own output) from harmful recursive contamination, creating systematic false positives when applied to curated synthetic data.
32	Binary features are designed for the human-vs.-synthetic boundary and are not expected to capture fine-grained depth differences, as the distributional shift between adjacent generations is orders of magnitude smaller than the shift between human and first-generation text.
33	Recent work moves beyond binary labels along other axes: \cite{cheng2025beyond} measure the degree of human--LLM collaboration, and \cite{mehta2025beyond} propose hierarchical contamination detection across four levels (none/paraphrase/synthetic/memorized).
34	Both pursue finer-grained characterization of synthetic text but along orthogonal dimensions---collaboration intensity and contamination type, respectively---whereas our depth axis captures recursive generation steps, a complementary facet that neither framework addresses.
35	
36	\paragraph{Ordinal Classification.}
37	Ordinal regression methods exploit the natural ordering among class labels to improve generalization over nominal classifiers.
38	Cao et al.~\cite{cao2020coral} introduced CORAL, which enforces rank consistency through weight sharing in the output layer, guaranteeing that predicted cumulative probabilities are monotonically non-increasing.
39	Ordinal approaches have been applied in NLP tasks such as sentiment intensity prediction and essay scoring, where adjacent categories share more semantic overlap than distant ones.
40	Generational depth exhibits the same ordinal structure: text at depth~$k$ is distributionally closer to depth~$k\!\pm\!1$ than to depth~$k\!\pm\!3$, because each recursive generation step introduces an incremental distributional shift rather than a discontinuous one.
41	Despite this natural fit, ordinal classification has not been applied to synthetic text depth estimation.
42	The idea of decomposing ordinal problems into a series of binary decisions dates to Frank \& Hall~\cite{frank2001ordinal}; our Ordinal Binary Decomposition (OBD) head follows this principle by learning $K\!-\!1$ cumulative boundary classifiers, yielding monotonic depth predictions and stronger calibration than a flat softmax baseline.
43	
44	\paragraph{Probing Classifiers.}
45	Linear and shallow MLP probes have become a standard tool for analyzing what information is encoded in pretrained representations~\cite{alain2017understanding,conneau2018probing}.
46	Belinkov~\cite{belinkov2022probing} surveys the methodology and cautions that probe complexity must be controlled to ensure that performance reflects representational content rather than probe capacity.
47	Our neural probe experiment follows this protocol: a two-layer MLP on frozen Qwen2.5-1.5B embeddings, where the probe's limited capacity ensures that discriminability reflects depth information already present in the representations rather than learned de novo.
48	
49	\paragraph{Data Selection and Curation.}
50	Principled data selection methods improve training corpus quality through distribution matching and deduplication.
51	DSIR~\cite{xie2023dsir} selects pretraining data by importance resampling against a target distribution.
52	D4~\cite{tirumala2023d4} combines deduplication with diversification to reduce redundancy, and DoReMi~\cite{xie2023doremi} learns domain weights via a proxy model to optimize downstream performance.
53	These methods operate on distributional properties of the corpus but do not estimate whether individual documents have undergone recursive generation.
54	
55	The closest prior work is Drayson et al.~\cite{drayson2025}, who combined binary machine-generated text detection with stratified importance resampling (SIR) to filter synthetic content and prevent model collapse.
56	Their approach is a special case of our graduated filtering framework: when $\Kstar = 1$, ordinal depth estimation reduces to binary classification, and depth-aware curation degenerates to their SIR-based scheme.
57	We generalize this binary formulation to ordinal depth estimation, enabling finer-grained curation that preserves mildly contaminated text (depth~1, retaining most original signal) while removing deeply corrupted text (depth~$\geq 2$).
58	Recent work demonstrates that external verification can prevent model collapse during recursive training~\citep{feng2025beyond}.
59	Yi et al.~\cite{yi2025escaping} formalize verifier-guided retraining and show that verification effectiveness is bounded by the verifier's knowledge; our $\Kstar$ can inform such verifiers by delineating the depth frontier below which quality discrimination remains feasible, positioning depth estimation as a natural verification signal for data curation.
60	Amin et al.~\cite{amin2025escaping} demonstrated that even weak quality signals suffice to escape model collapse when applied iteratively, suggesting that approximate depth estimates beyond $\Kempirical$ may remain practically useful.
61	Gambetta et al.~\cite{gambetta2025surplexity} proposed surplexity as a text quality metric correlated with generative degradation, though without explicit depth calibration.
62	
63	\paragraph{Watermarking and Provenance.}
64	An alternative approach embeds identifiers at generation time.
65	Kirchenbauer et al.~\cite{kirchenbauer2023watermark} proposed statistical watermarking for LLM outputs by partitioning the vocabulary into green and red token lists conditioned on preceding context.
66	Watermarking is complementary to depth estimation: it requires control over the generation process and cooperation from providers, whereas our method operates post-hoc on unwatermarked text.
67	The two approaches address different threat models---watermarking assumes a cooperative generator, while depth estimation targets uncontrolled settings where provenance metadata is unavailable.

% Sources: exp_007 (bootstrap CI + permutation), exp_001/exp_002/exp_017/mvp_pilot (model-mode), exp_003 (decoding ablation)
We presented the first systematic measurement of the generational depth
discrimination boundary $\Kempirical$ for recursive synthetic text.
Across three model architectures in four model-mode configurations
(Pythia-1.4B and OLMo-1B in continuation mode; Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct in both
continuation and rewrite modes) and 4 decoding strategies---totaling 8
conditions---we establish $\Kempirical = 2$ as a consistent boundary:
classifiers reliably distinguish adjacent generations up to depth~2, but all
deeper pairs fall below the operational threshold $\theta = 0.60$.
For the four model-mode configurations, bootstrap 95\% confidence intervals
and permutation tests confirm statistical significance at the 1v2 boundary
($p \leq 0.002$ for all four); the most marginal case, Qwen-continuation,
yields a CI lower bound of 0.6015, exceeding $\theta$ by only 0.15\,pp.
All four decoding configurations (greedy, nucleus, $T{=}0.70$, $T{=}1.2$)
likewise yield 1v2 point-estimate $\auc$ above $\theta$.
The 0v1 boundary is near-perfectly separable ($\auc > 0.99$), followed by a
sharp ${\sim}$30\,pp drop at 1v2 ($\auc$: 0.6112--0.7039 across all
conditions), while all 2v3 pairs fall below~$\theta$.
Recursive generation thus acts as a severely lossy channel whose discriminable
statistical fingerprint is exhausted within two steps.

% === Contribution 2: Ordinal depth estimation framework ===
% Sources: exp_010 (OBD vs baselines), exp_013 (cross-model transfer), exp_005 (feature degradation), exp_011 (LLM zero-shot)
To operationalize depth estimation, we introduced an ordinal binary
decomposition (OBD) framework pairing 15 hand-crafted statistical features
with LightGBM classifiers.
Cross-model transfer experiments demonstrate 80--92\% accuracy retention
across continuation-mode model pairs, with
Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo achieving 90--92\% and 0v1 transfer $\auc$
exceeding 0.96 across all tested model pairs---indicating that depth signals are largely
text-intrinsic rather than generator-specific.
Feature degradation orderings are consistent across architectures
(Spearman $\rho \geq 0.85$), with surprisal-variance features dominating
across all tested families, suggesting that the two-step information loss is driven primarily by the
autoregressive mechanism at this scale.
As a reference point, frontier LLMs (GPT-5.5, Claude Opus~4.6) achieve
${\sim}$88\% binary human-vs.-synthetic accuracy but only ${\sim}$33\% on
5-class depth estimation, below OBD-LightGBM's 38.6\%---confirming that
fine-grained depth discrimination requires specialized statistical features
rather than general language understanding.
A preliminary neural probing experiment suggests that this operational bound is not tight: a frozen Qwen2.5-1.5B encoder paired with an MLP classifier achieves $\Kempirical^{\text{neural}} = 3$ on the Qwen-continuation dataset (2v3 $\auc = 0.6195$ versus 0.5609 with hand-crafted features), indicating that learned representations recover depth signal beyond the 15-dimensional feature set.
This result, pending cross-model validation, provides initial evidence that $\Ktheory \geq 3$.

% === Contribution 3: Graduated filtering (C3) ===
% Source: exp_006 (RUNNING — results pending)
The $\Kempirical = 2$ boundary implies a natural trichotomy---human (depth~0), first-generation synthetic (depth~1), and deeper synthetic (depth~$\geq 2$)---that can be exploited for depth-aware data curation.
% TODO: exp-006 graduated filtering 具体结果填充。
% 预留内容：graduated filtering 利用三级分类法在 MMLU/HellaSwag 上的表现，
% 与 binary filtering 和 no-filter baseline 的对比。

% === Limitations + Future Work ===
Our findings are bounded by the scale of models tested ($\leq$1.5B parameters), restriction to English C4 text, and the use of prompt-chain rather than retrain-chain protocols; $\Kempirical$ depends on the threshold $\theta$ and shifts with generation mode (continuation-mode configurations drop to $\Kempirical{=}1$ at $\theta{=}0.65$, while rewrite mode retains $\Kempirical{=}2$; Section~\ref{sec:limitations}); the 15-dimensional feature set yields $\Kempirical$ as an operational lower bound, and $\Ktheory$ may be strictly higher.
Several directions merit investigation: scaling to larger models (7B+) to test whether increased generation fidelity shifts the boundary; extending to multilingual and multi-domain corpora; establishing the relationship between prompt-chain and retrain-chain $\Kstar$ values, which would connect our measurements to the model collapse setting; incorporating few-shot or chain-of-thought prompting for LLM-based depth estimation; and extending the neural probe approach---which has yielded preliminary evidence of $\Kempirical^{\text{neural}} = 3$ on one dataset---through cross-model validation (Pythia, OLMo), bootstrap confidence intervals, multi-layer probing beyond the last hidden state, and comparison with fine-tuned (non-frozen) encoders to further narrow the gap between $\Kempirical$ and $\Ktheory$.

1	\section{Experiments}
2	\label{sec:experiments}
3	
4	We evaluate generational depth estimation on four model configurations:
5	Pythia-1.4B and OLMo-1B in continuation mode, and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct in both rewrite and continuation modes.
6	All experiments use the OBD-LightGBM classifier with the 15-dimensional feature set described in Section~\ref{sec:method}.
7	Each configuration uses a balanced corpus of 5{,}000 texts per depth level (generations 0--5).
8	We organize results around four questions:
9	(1)~Does $\Kempirical = 2$ hold across configurations?
10	(2)~Do depth classifiers transfer across models?
11	(3)~Is the feature degradation ordering model-independent?
12	(4)~How does generation mode affect detectability?
13	
14	%% ====================================================================
15	\subsection{$\Kempirical = 2$ Across All Configurations}
16	\label{sec:kstar_boundary}
17	
18	Table~\ref{tab:kstar_ci} reports pairwise $\auc$ for adjacent depth pairs
19	across all four configurations, with bootstrap 95\% confidence intervals
20	(1{,}000 resamples) and permutation-test $p$-values for the critical 1v2
21	and 2v3 boundaries.
22	
23	\begin{table}[t]
24	\centering
25	\small
26	\caption{Pairwise $\auc$ for adjacent depth pairs.  Bootstrap 95\% CIs
27	and permutation $p$-values shown for the $\Kstar$ boundary rows (1v2,
28	2v3).  $\Kempirical = 2$ requires 1v2 $\text{CI}_\text{low} > \theta$
29	and 2v3 $\text{CI}_\text{high} < \theta$ with $\theta = 0.60$.
30	All 0v1 permutation $p \leq 0.002$ (Qwen-continuation 0v1: CI [0.9963, 0.9978], $p = 0.002$).}
31	\label{tab:kstar_ci}
32	\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
33	\toprule
34	 & Qwen-rw & Pythia & OLMo & Qwen-cont \\
35	\midrule
36	0v1 & 0.9956 & 0.9932 & 0.9970 & 0.9971 \\[4pt]
37	1v2 & 0.6955 & 0.6539 & 0.6145 & 0.6112 \\
38	{\footnotesize CI}
39	  & {\footnotesize [.6859,\,.7041]}
40	  & {\footnotesize [.6454,\,.6630]}
41	  & {\footnotesize [.6045,\,.6247]}
42	  & {\footnotesize [.6015,\,.6213]} \\
43	{\footnotesize $p$}
44	  & {\footnotesize .002}
45	  & {\footnotesize .002}
46	  & {\footnotesize .002}
47	  & {\footnotesize .002} \\[4pt]
48	2v3 & 0.5893 & 0.5514 & 0.5496 & 0.5609 \\
49	{\footnotesize CI}
50	  & {\footnotesize [.5795,\,.5991]}
51	  & {\footnotesize [.5417,\,.5628]}
52	  & {\footnotesize [.5399,\,.5596]}
53	  & {\footnotesize [.5511,\,.5712]} \\
54	{\footnotesize $p$}
55	  & {\footnotesize .002}
56	  & {\footnotesize .002}
57	  & {\footnotesize .002}
58	  & {\footnotesize .002} \\[4pt]
59	3v4 & 0.5435 & 0.5152 & 0.5091 & 0.5409 \\
60	4v5 & 0.5340 & 0.5136 & 0.5045 & 0.5141 \\
61	\bottomrule
62	\end{tabular}
63	\end{table}
64	
65	The pattern is consistent across all four configurations:
66	0v1 discrimination is near-perfect ($\auc > 0.99$),
67	followed by a sharp drop at 1v2 ($\auc$ range: 0.6112--0.6955),
68	with 2v3 falling below the decision threshold $\theta = 0.60$
69	($\auc$ range: 0.5496--0.5893).
70	All subsequent pairs (3v4, 4v5) converge toward chance.
71	Figure~\ref{fig:auc_decay} visualizes this decay.
72	
73	\begin{figure}[t]
74	\centering
75	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig2_auc_decay.pdf}
76	\caption{Pairwise $\auc$ as a function of depth pair across four model-mode configurations (solid) and four decoding strategies (dashed).  All configurations show a sharp drop between 0v1 and 1v2, with 2v3 and deeper pairs falling below the decision threshold $\theta = 0.60$ (horizontal dashed line).  Error bars show bootstrap 95\% CIs for model-mode configurations; decoding strategy curves omit CIs as they were computed on a separate experimental setup.}
77	\label{fig:auc_decay}
78	\end{figure}
79	
80	For the $\Kempirical$ determination, all four 1v2 CI lower bounds exceed
81	$\theta$: Qwen-rewrite ($\text{CI}_\text{low} = 0.6859$), Pythia (0.6454),
82	OLMo (0.6045), and Qwen-continuation (0.6015).
83	Conversely, all four 2v3 CI upper bounds fall below $\theta$:
84	Qwen-rewrite ($\text{CI}_\text{high} = 0.5991$), Qwen-continuation (0.5712),
85	Pythia (0.5628), and OLMo (0.5596).
86	Permutation tests confirm $p = 0.002$ for all eight boundary comparisons.
87	Together these establish $\Kempirical = 2$ as a consistent discrimination boundary across all tested configurations at the $\leq$1.5B scale.
88	
89	The most marginal case is Qwen-continuation, where the 1v2 CI lower bound
90	(0.6015) exceeds $\theta$ by only 0.0015.  This narrow margin
91	indicates that $\Kempirical = 2$ is robust but not trivially so---continuation-mode
92	generation produces weaker depth artifacts than rewrite mode, pushing the
93	boundary closer to the detection threshold.
94	
95	The absolute 1v2 $\auc$ varies across models:
96	Qwen-rewrite (0.6955) $>$ Pythia (0.6539) $>$ OLMo (0.6145) $\approx$ Qwen-continuation (0.6112).
97	Notably, the spread due to generation mode within a single model
98	(Qwen-rewrite vs.\ Qwen-continuation: $\Delta = 8.4$\,pp) exceeds the spread
99	across models in the same mode
100	(Pythia vs.\ OLMo: $\Delta = 3.9$\,pp),
101	suggesting that generation protocol is a stronger determinant
102	of detectability than model identity.
103	We examine both factors in Sections~\ref{sec:transfer}
104	and~\ref{sec:generation_mode}.
105	
106	Beyond the $\Kempirical$ boundary, depth discrimination deteriorates
107	rapidly.
108	OLMo shows nonsignificant permutation $p$-values at 3v4
109	($p = 0.064$) and 4v5 ($p = 0.232$), indicating that depth
110	classification beyond generation~2 is indistinguishable from
111	random for this model.
112	Pythia retains marginal effects at these depths
113	($p = 0.006$ and $p = 0.008$, respectively),
114	while Qwen-continuation shows weak but detectable discrimination through
115	3v4 ($p = 0.002$) that fades at 4v5 ($p = 0.006$).
116	
117	\paragraph{Classifier design justification.}
118	The OBD formulation is motivated by a three-way comparison with multiclass LightGBM and ordinal logistic regression (Section~\ref{sec:method}).
119	Across all three model families, OBD achieves the best accuracy (38.2--42.3\%, i.e., $+$21.5--25.6\,pp over the 16.7\% random baseline for 6-class classification, and $+$5.5\,pp over frontier-LLM zero-shot on the matched 5-class task, 38.6\% vs.\ ${\sim}$33\%; cf.\ Table~\ref{tab:s3_llm_zeroshot}) while maintaining competitive MAE.
120	Ordinal logistic regression yields the lowest MAE (e.g., 0.911 vs.\ 0.984 OBD on Qwen-rewrite) but at the cost of near-chance pairwise AUC (mean 0.49 vs.\ 0.61 for OBD across families)---it reduces error by collapsing predictions toward central depths rather than genuinely distinguishing adjacent levels.
121	Multiclass LightGBM matches OBD on pairwise AUC but consistently trails in both accuracy and MAE.
122	OBD thus provides the best balance across all three evaluation axes, justifying its use as the default classifier throughout.
123	
124	%% ====================================================================
125	\subsection{Cross-Model Transfer}
126	\label{sec:transfer}
127	
128	Having established $\Kempirical = 2$ consistently, we next ask: is this boundary a property of the text itself, or an artifact of model self-familiarity?
129	To answer this, we train classifiers on one model's outputs and evaluate on another's.
130	Table~\ref{tab:transfer_matrix} shows the full
131	$4 \times 4$ transfer accuracy matrix for 6-class ordinal depth
132	classification.
133	
134	\begin{table}[t]
135	\centering
136	\small
137	\caption{Cross-model transfer accuracy (6-class ordinal
138	classification).  Diagonal entries (bold): within-model accuracy.
139	Off-diagonal: cross-model transfer.  Retention is computed as
140	off-diagonal accuracy divided by the diagonal entry of the training
141	model.}
142	\label{tab:transfer_matrix}
143	\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
144	\toprule
145	Train $\downarrow$ / Test $\rightarrow$
146	  & Qwen-rw & Pythia & OLMo & Qwen-cont \\
147	\midrule
148	Qwen-rw
149	  & \textbf{0.4229} & 0.2590 & 0.2653 & 0.3466 \\
150	Pythia
151	  & 0.2718 & \textbf{0.3856} & 0.3531 & 0.3287 \\
152	OLMo
153	  & 0.2768 & 0.3450 & \textbf{0.3822} & 0.3244 \\
154	Qwen-cont
155	  & 0.3440 & 0.3284 & 0.3112 & \textbf{0.3875} \\
156	\bottomrule
157	\end{tabular}
158	\end{table}
159	
160	\begin{figure}[t]
161	\centering
162	\includegraphics[width=0.85\columnwidth]{figures/fig3_transfer_heatmap.pdf}
163	\caption{Cross-model transfer heatmap (6-class ordinal accuracy).
164	Rows: training model; columns: test model.
165	Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo (both continuation mode) shows high
166	mutual transfer (90--92\% accuracy retention), while Qwen-rewrite
167	transfers poorly to continuation-mode models (61--63\%).
168	Diagonal entries are within-model baselines.}
169	\label{fig:transfer_heatmap}
170	\end{figure}
171	
172	Two principal findings emerge (Figure~\ref{fig:transfer_heatmap}).
173	First, transfer between continuation-mode models is high.
174	Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo mutual transfer retains 90--92\% of within-model accuracy
175	(85--86\% retention by Kendall $\tau$).
176	The accuracy-based retention of 90--92\% is complemented by the
177	$\tau$-based retention of 85--86\%, indicating that not only
178	classification accuracy but also the relative depth ordering of
179	predictions is largely preserved.
180	Qwen-continuation$\leftrightarrow$Pythia also transfers well
181	(84--85\% accuracy retention),
182	and Qwen-continuation$\leftrightarrow$OLMo achieves 80--85\%.
183	These retention rates---80--92\% of within-model accuracy preserved across continuation-mode pairs---suggest that a large component of the depth signal is text-intrinsic rather than tied to a specific generator.
184	
185	Second, Qwen-rewrite exhibits catastrophic transfer failure.
186	Classifiers trained on Qwen-rewrite retain only 61--63\% of
187	within-model accuracy when evaluated on Pythia or OLMo
188	(45--50\% by $\tau$).
189	The reverse direction transfers asymmetrically: Pythia/OLMo${\to}$Qwen-rewrite retains 70--72\% of within-model accuracy, higher than the forward 61--63\% but still far below continuation-mode transfer rates (80--92\%).
190	This confirms that rewrite-mode classifiers rely on generation
191	artifacts that do not generalize across models, in contrast
192	to Qwen-continuation, which achieves 80--85\% retention to the same targets.
193	
194	At the 0v1 boundary, cross-model pairwise $\auc$ exceeds 0.96
195	for all model pairs, confirming that the human-vs.-synthetic
196	distinction is consistently transferable across all tested generators
197	and modes.
198	The transfer degradation concentrates at deeper boundaries
199	(1v2 and beyond), where model- and mode-specific factors dominate.
200	
201	The aggregate picture is one of modest cross-model loss:
202	mean pairwise $\auc$ is 0.6099 within-model versus 0.5905
203	cross-model.
204	This gap is driven primarily by Qwen-rewrite; among
205	continuation-mode pairs the within/cross difference narrows
206	further.
207	
208	%% ====================================================================
209	\subsection{Feature Degradation Ordering}
210	\label{sec:feature_degradation}
211	
212	The transfer results indicate that depth signals are largely text-intrinsic.
213	We next ask what drives discrimination: if the signal is text-intrinsic, different generators should rely on the same features in the same order.
214	We test this by computing single-feature $\auc$ rankings
215	independently for each model and comparing them via rank
216	correlation.
217	
218	\begin{table}[t]
219	\centering
220	\small
221	\caption{Top-3 features by single-feature $\auc$ ranking for each
222	model configuration.
223	Features shared across all three continuation-mode models are in bold.
224	Qwen-rewrite's top feature (\texttt{freq\_entropy}) is mode-specific.
225	Spearman $\rho$ (continuation-mode pairs): Pythia--OLMo 0.95,
226	Pythia--Qwen-continuation 0.9143, OLMo--Qwen-continuation 0.85.}
227	\label{tab:top_features}
228	\begin{tabular}{cllll}
229	\toprule
230	Rank & Pythia & OLMo & Qwen-rw & Qwen-cont \\
231	\midrule
232	1
233	  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}}
234	  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_std}}
235	  & \texttt{freq\_entropy}
236	  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}} \\
237	2
238	  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d2\_std}}
239	  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}}
240	  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_std}}
241	  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_std}} \\
242	3
243	  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_std}}
244	  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d2\_std}}
245	  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}}
246	  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d2\_std}} \\
247	\bottomrule
248	\end{tabular}
249	\end{table}
250	
251	Among continuation-mode models, single-feature $\auc$ rankings
252	are highly correlated:
253	Pythia vs.\ OLMo $\rho = 0.95$,
254	Pythia vs.\ Qwen-continuation $\rho = 0.9143$,
255	OLMo vs.\ Qwen-continuation $\rho = 0.85$
256	(all $\rho \geq 0.85$).
257	The top-3 features---\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}, \texttt{surp\_std},
258	and \texttt{surp\_d2\_std}---are shared (up to ordering) across
259	all three continuation-mode configurations
260	(Table~\ref{tab:top_features}).
261	All three measure variability of surprisal or its derivatives,
262	capturing the \emph{heterogeneity} of token-level predictability
263	across the text.
264	That these features degrade in a shared order across generators
265	suggests a common mechanism: each generation step smooths the
266	token-level surprisal landscape, reducing its variance in a
267	model-independent fashion.
268	
269	Qwen-rewrite diverges: its top-ranked feature is
270	\texttt{freq\_entropy}, a lexical diversity measure absent from
271	the continuation-mode top-3 for any model.
272	This corroborates the transfer results in
273	Section~\ref{sec:transfer}---rewrite-mode classifiers learn
274	partly from instruction-following artifacts rather than the
275	shared surprisal-based signals.
276	
277	Kendall $\tau$ provides a complementary, more conservative
278	perspective:
279	Pythia vs.\ OLMo $\tau = 0.733$,
280	Pythia vs.\ Qwen-continuation $\tau = 0.695$,
281	OLMo vs.\ Qwen-continuation $\tau = 0.543$.
282	Cross-mode correlations are lower:
283	Pythia vs.\ Qwen-rewrite $\tau = 0.467$,
284	OLMo vs.\ Qwen-rewrite $\tau = 0.429$.
285	
286	\paragraph{Limitation.}
287	The high Spearman $\rho$ characterizes the \emph{aggregate}
288	feature ranking, but at the depth-pair level the agreement
289	weakens: $\tau \approx 0.37$ at the 1v2 boundary.
290	This means that while the overall importance ordering is shared,
291	the relative contribution of individual features at the
292	discrimination boundary---where precision matters most---varies
293	across models.
294	We view this as a genuine limitation of the text-intrinsic
295	interpretation and a direction for future investigation.
296	
297	%% ====================================================================
298	\subsection{Generation Mode Effect}
299	\label{sec:generation_mode}
300	
301	Finally, we ask whether generation mode---an experimental design choice rather than a text property---affects depth detectability.
302	Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct provides a controlled comparison: rewrite (instruction-based paraphrasing) and continuation (prompt truncation) share the same model weights, as defined in Section~\ref{sec:method}, isolating the effect of generation protocol.
303	
304	Rewrite mode yields higher 1v2 $\auc$ than continuation:
305	0.6955 vs.\ 0.6112, a difference of $+$8.4 percentage points.
306	The advantage persists at 2v3
307	(0.5893 vs.\ 0.5609, $\Delta = +$2.8\,pp)
308	and narrows at 3v4
309	(0.5435 vs.\ 0.5409, $\Delta = +$0.3\,pp),
310	with both modes converging toward chance at deeper levels.
311	The amplified detectability under rewrite mode is consistent
312	with instruction-following introducing systematic deviations
313	from the source text's style---additional artifacts that are
314	discriminable but mode-specific rather than text-intrinsic.
315	
316	Transfer between modes is asymmetric.
317	A classifier trained on Qwen-continuation and evaluated on Qwen-rewrite
318	retains 89\% of within-model accuracy
319	(0.3440 vs.\ 0.3875 diagonal),
320	whereas the reverse direction---Qwen-rewrite trained,
321	Qwen-continuation tested---retains 82\%
322	(0.3466 vs.\ 0.4229 diagonal).
323	The direction of the asymmetry is intuitive:
324	continuation-mode signals form a subset of the information
325	available in rewrite-mode data
326	(which adds instruction-following artifacts on top),
327	so a continuation-trained classifier can partially recognize
328	rewrite-mode outputs but not vice versa.
329	
330	This asymmetry is mirrored in the feature rankings.
331	Qwen-rewrite's top feature (\texttt{freq\_entropy}) is
332	mode-specific and ranks outside the top-3 for every
333	continuation-mode model.
334	Qwen-continuation's top feature (\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}) is shared
335	with Pythia and OLMo, confirming that continuation mode
336	captures primarily text-intrinsic depth signals.
337	
338	The practical implication is a detectability--generalizability
339	tradeoff.
340	Rewrite-mode classifiers achieve higher absolute $\auc$ but
341	transfer poorly across models
342	(Qwen-rewrite$\to$Pythia/OLMo: 61--63\% retention).
343	Continuation-mode classifiers sacrifice 8.4\,pp of within-model
344	$\auc$ but achieve robust cross-model transfer
345	(Qwen-continuation$\to$Pythia: 84--85\%).
346	For deployment scenarios requiring model-agnostic depth
347	estimation, continuation-mode features provide a more reliable
348	foundation despite lower raw discriminability.
349	
350	%% ====================================================================
351	\subsection{Representation Dependence of $\Kempirical$}
352	\label{sec:neural_probe}
353	
354	The preceding sections establish $\Kempirical = 2$ using a 15-dimensional hand-crafted feature set.
355	A natural question is whether this boundary reflects a fundamental limit of the generational depth signal or an information bottleneck imposed by projecting high-dimensional text representations into 15 statistical summaries.
356	To disentangle these possibilities, we replace the hand-crafted features with frozen LLM hidden states and train a lightweight MLP probe on the same classification task.
357	
358	\paragraph{Setup.}
359	We extract last-layer hidden states from a frozen Qwen2.5-1.5B model (\texttt{float16}), apply attention-masked average pooling to obtain 1536-dimensional document embeddings, and train a two-hidden-layer MLP ($1536 \to 512 \to 256 \to 6$, ReLU, dropout 0.1) with 5-fold GroupKFold cross-validation on the Qwen-continuation dataset (Table~\ref{tab:s7_neural_probe}).
360	The probe's limited capacity ensures that any discriminability reflects depth information already encoded in the frozen representations rather than patterns learned de novo.
361	% TODO(exp-015-rerun): Pythia/OLMo neural probe setup details here
362	
363	\paragraph{Results.}
364	% TODO(exp-015-rerun): cross-model neural probe comparison table
365	Preliminary results on the Qwen-continuation dataset are reported below; cross-model validation on Pythia and OLMo is pending.
366	The neural probe achieves 6-class accuracy of 0.4335 (vs.\ 0.3875 for LightGBM with 15D features).
367	The pairwise $\auc$ profile reveals a shifted discrimination boundary:
368	\begin{center}
369	\small
370	\begin{tabular}{lccccc}
371	\toprule
372	 & 0v1 & 1v2 & 2v3 & 3v4 & 4v5 \\
373	\midrule
374	15D (LightGBM)   & 0.997 & 0.611 & 0.561 & 0.541 & 0.514 \\
375	Neural (MLP)      & 0.987 & 0.698 & 0.620 & 0.593 & 0.575 \\
376	$\Delta$\,(pp)    & $-$1.0 & $+$8.7 & $+$5.9 & $+$5.2 & $+$6.1 \\
377	\bottomrule
378	\end{tabular}
379	\end{center}
380	The neural probe's 2v3 $\auc = 0.6195$ ($\text{std} = 0.0094$ across folds) exceeds $\theta = 0.60$, yielding $\Kempirical^{\text{neural}} = 3$---one discriminable boundary beyond what the 15D feature set recovers on the same data.
381	The 15D classifier on the same dataset gives 2v3 $\auc = 0.5609$ (Section~\ref{sec:kstar_boundary}), well below $\theta$.
382	The improvement concentrates at the 1v2 and 2v3 boundaries ($+$8.7 and $+$5.9\,pp, respectively), where the 15D features lose most of their discriminative power; at the already-trivial 0v1 boundary the neural probe is marginally \emph{lower} ($-$1.0\,pp), consistent with both representations saturating the human--synthetic gap.
383	At 3v4, the neural probe reaches $\auc = 0.5930$---below $\theta$ but closer to the threshold than any 15D configuration---hinting that a still richer representation might push the boundary further.
384	
385	\paragraph{Interpretation: $\Kstar$ hierarchy.}
386	These preliminary results motivate a three-level hierarchy of discrimination boundaries:
387	\[
388	  \Ktheory \;\geq\; \Kempirical^{\text{neural}} \;\geq\; \Kempirical^{\text{15D}}
389	\]
390	where $\Kempirical^{\text{15D}} = 2$ is the operationally deployable boundary measured with model-free, interpretable features, and $\Kempirical^{\text{neural}} = 3$ is a representation-dependent ceiling accessible only through model-specific probing.
391	The gap between the two confirms that the 15D feature set does not saturate the available depth signal: at least one additional discriminable generation boundary exists in the frozen representations but is lost during projection into the hand-crafted feature space.
392	The theoretical upper bound $\Ktheory$---the boundary achievable with an optimal representation and classifier---remains unknown but is at least~3.
393	
394	\paragraph{Interpretability--discriminability tradeoff.}
395	The two $\Kempirical$ estimates serve complementary purposes.
396	The 15D boundary ($\Kempirical = 2$) is model-free, interpretable, and computationally lightweight: features are extracted from surface-level token statistics without access to model internals, and the LightGBM classifier trains in seconds.
397	This makes it suitable for deployment in data curation pipelines.
398	The neural boundary ($\Kempirical^{\text{neural}} = 3$) requires a frozen copy of a specific LLM for embedding extraction, is opaque in the features it exploits, and incurs $100\times$+ computational overhead for inference.
399	It is valuable as a theoretical exploration tool---demonstrating that deeper depth signals \emph{exist}---but impractical for the model-agnostic deployment scenarios where depth estimation is most needed.
400	Notably, the neural probe's advantage does not alter the headline result for practitioners: $\Kempirical = 2$ remains the relevant boundary for deployable depth estimation with current feature technology.
401	
402	\paragraph{Caveats.}
403	The 2v3 boundary under neural probing is marginal: the mean $\auc$ of 0.6195 exceeds $\theta = 0.60$ by only $+$1.95\,pp, and individual fold variation (std $= 0.0094$) places this margin within approximately two standard deviations of the threshold.
404	These results should be treated as preliminary evidence that the 15D boundary is representation-dependent, not as a firm revision of $\Kempirical$.

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

We evaluate generational depth estimation on four model configurations:
Pythia-1.4B and OLMo-1B in continuation mode, and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct in both rewrite and continuation modes.
All experiments use the OBD-LightGBM classifier with the 15-dimensional feature set described in Section~\ref{sec:method}.
Each configuration uses a balanced corpus of 5{,}000 texts per depth level (generations 0--5).
We organize results around four questions:
(1)~Does $\Kempirical = 2$ hold across configurations?
(2)~Do depth classifiers transfer across models?
(3)~Is the feature degradation ordering model-independent?
(4)~How does generation mode affect detectability?

%% ====================================================================
\subsection{$\Kempirical = 2$ Across All Configurations}
\label{sec:kstar_boundary}

Table~\ref{tab:kstar_ci} reports pairwise $\auc$ for adjacent depth pairs
across all four configurations, with bootstrap 95\% confidence intervals
(1{,}000 resamples) and permutation-test $p$-values for the critical 1v2
and 2v3 boundaries.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Pairwise $\auc$ for adjacent depth pairs.  Bootstrap 95\% CIs
and permutation $p$-values shown for the $\Kstar$ boundary rows (1v2,
2v3).  $\Kempirical = 2$ requires 1v2 $\text{CI}_\text{low} > \theta$
and 2v3 $\text{CI}_\text{high} < \theta$ with $\theta = 0.60$.
All 0v1 permutation $p \leq 0.002$ (Qwen-continuation 0v1: CI [0.9963, 0.9978], $p = 0.002$).}
\label{tab:kstar_ci}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
 & Qwen-rw & Pythia & OLMo & Qwen-cont \\
\midrule
0v1 & 0.9956 & 0.9932 & 0.9970 & 0.9971 \\[4pt]
1v2 & 0.6955 & 0.6539 & 0.6145 & 0.6112 \\
{\footnotesize CI}
  & {\footnotesize [.6859,\,.7041]}
  & {\footnotesize [.6454,\,.6630]}
  & {\footnotesize [.6045,\,.6247]}
  & {\footnotesize [.6015,\,.6213]} \\
{\footnotesize $p$}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002} \\[4pt]
2v3 & 0.5893 & 0.5514 & 0.5496 & 0.5609 \\
{\footnotesize CI}
  & {\footnotesize [.5795,\,.5991]}
  & {\footnotesize [.5417,\,.5628]}
  & {\footnotesize [.5399,\,.5596]}
  & {\footnotesize [.5511,\,.5712]} \\
{\footnotesize $p$}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002} \\[4pt]
3v4 & 0.5435 & 0.5152 & 0.5091 & 0.5409 \\
4v5 & 0.5340 & 0.5136 & 0.5045 & 0.5141 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The pattern is consistent across all four configurations:
0v1 discrimination is near-perfect ($\auc > 0.99$),
followed by a sharp drop at 1v2 ($\auc$ range: 0.6112--0.6955),
with 2v3 falling below the decision threshold $\theta = 0.60$
($\auc$ range: 0.5496--0.5893).
All subsequent pairs (3v4, 4v5) converge toward chance.
Figure~\ref{fig:auc_decay} visualizes this decay.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig2_auc_decay.pdf}
\caption{Pairwise $\auc$ as a function of depth pair across four model-mode configurations (solid) and four decoding strategies (dashed).  All configurations show a sharp drop between 0v1 and 1v2, with 2v3 and deeper pairs falling below the decision threshold $\theta = 0.60$ (horizontal dashed line).  Error bars show bootstrap 95\% CIs for model-mode configurations; decoding strategy curves omit CIs as they were computed on a separate experimental setup.}
\label{fig:auc_decay}
\end{figure}

For the $\Kempirical$ determination, all four 1v2 CI lower bounds exceed
$\theta$: Qwen-rewrite ($\text{CI}_\text{low} = 0.6859$), Pythia (0.6454),
OLMo (0.6045), and Qwen-continuation (0.6015).
Conversely, all four 2v3 CI upper bounds fall below $\theta$:
Qwen-rewrite ($\text{CI}_\text{high} = 0.5991$), Qwen-continuation (0.5712),
Pythia (0.5628), and OLMo (0.5596).
Permutation tests confirm $p = 0.002$ for all eight boundary comparisons.
Together these establish $\Kempirical = 2$ as a consistent discrimination boundary across all tested configurations at the $\leq$1.5B scale.

The most marginal case is Qwen-continuation, where the 1v2 CI lower bound
(0.6015) exceeds $\theta$ by only 0.0015.  This narrow margin
indicates that $\Kempirical = 2$ is robust but not trivially so---continuation-mode
generation produces weaker depth artifacts than rewrite mode, pushing the
boundary closer to the detection threshold.

The absolute 1v2 $\auc$ varies across models:
Qwen-rewrite (0.6955) $>$ Pythia (0.6539) $>$ OLMo (0.6145) $\approx$ Qwen-continuation (0.6112).
Notably, the spread due to generation mode within a single model
(Qwen-rewrite vs.\ Qwen-continuation: $\Delta = 8.4$\,pp) exceeds the spread
across models in the same mode
(Pythia vs.\ OLMo: $\Delta = 3.9$\,pp),
suggesting that generation protocol is a stronger determinant
of detectability than model identity.
We examine both factors in Sections~\ref{sec:transfer}
and~\ref{sec:generation_mode}.

Beyond the $\Kempirical$ boundary, depth discrimination deteriorates
rapidly.
OLMo shows nonsignificant permutation $p$-values at 3v4
($p = 0.064$) and 4v5 ($p = 0.232$), indicating that depth
classification beyond generation~2 is indistinguishable from
random for this model.
Pythia retains marginal effects at these depths
($p = 0.006$ and $p = 0.008$, respectively),
while Qwen-continuation shows weak but detectable discrimination through
3v4 ($p = 0.002$) that fades at 4v5 ($p = 0.006$).

\paragraph{Classifier design justification.}
The OBD formulation is motivated by a three-way comparison with multiclass LightGBM and ordinal logistic regression (Section~\ref{sec:method}).
Across all three model families, OBD achieves the best accuracy (38.2--42.3\%, i.e., $+$21.5--25.6\,pp over the 16.7\% random baseline for 6-class classification, and $+$5.5\,pp over frontier-LLM zero-shot on the matched 5-class task, 38.6\% vs.\ ${\sim}$33\%; cf.\ Table~\ref{tab:s3_llm_zeroshot}) while maintaining competitive MAE.
Ordinal logistic regression yields the lowest MAE (e.g., 0.911 vs.\ 0.984 OBD on Qwen-rewrite) but at the cost of near-chance pairwise AUC (mean 0.49 vs.\ 0.61 for OBD across families)---it reduces error by collapsing predictions toward central depths rather than genuinely distinguishing adjacent levels.
Multiclass LightGBM matches OBD on pairwise AUC but consistently trails in both accuracy and MAE.
OBD thus provides the best balance across all three evaluation axes, justifying its use as the default classifier throughout.

%% ====================================================================
\subsection{Cross-Model Transfer}
\label{sec:transfer}

Having established $\Kempirical = 2$ consistently, we next ask: is this boundary a property of the text itself, or an artifact of model self-familiarity?
To answer this, we train classifiers on one model's outputs and evaluate on another's.
Table~\ref{tab:transfer_matrix} shows the full
$4 \times 4$ transfer accuracy matrix for 6-class ordinal depth
classification.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Cross-model transfer accuracy (6-class ordinal
classification).  Diagonal entries (bold): within-model accuracy.
Off-diagonal: cross-model transfer.  Retention is computed as
off-diagonal accuracy divided by the diagonal entry of the training
model.}
\label{tab:transfer_matrix}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
Train $\downarrow$ / Test $\rightarrow$
  & Qwen-rw & Pythia & OLMo & Qwen-cont \\
\midrule
Qwen-rw
  & \textbf{0.4229} & 0.2590 & 0.2653 & 0.3466 \\
Pythia
  & 0.2718 & \textbf{0.3856} & 0.3531 & 0.3287 \\
OLMo
  & 0.2768 & 0.3450 & \textbf{0.3822} & 0.3244 \\
Qwen-cont
  & 0.3440 & 0.3284 & 0.3112 & \textbf{0.3875} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.85\columnwidth]{figures/fig3_transfer_heatmap.pdf}
\caption{Cross-model transfer heatmap (6-class ordinal accuracy).
Rows: training model; columns: test model.
Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo (both continuation mode) shows high
mutual transfer (90--92\% accuracy retention), while Qwen-rewrite
transfers poorly to continuation-mode models (61--63\%).
Diagonal entries are within-model baselines.}
\label{fig:transfer_heatmap}
\end{figure}

Two principal findings emerge (Figure~\ref{fig:transfer_heatmap}).
First, transfer between continuation-mode models is high.
Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo mutual transfer retains 90--92\% of within-model accuracy
(85--86\% retention by Kendall $\tau$).
The accuracy-based retention of 90--92\% is complemented by the
$\tau$-based retention of 85--86\%, indicating that not only
classification accuracy but also the relative depth ordering of
predictions is largely preserved.
Qwen-continuation$\leftrightarrow$Pythia also transfers well
(84--85\% accuracy retention),
and Qwen-continuation$\leftrightarrow$OLMo achieves 80--85\%.
These retention rates---80--92\% of within-model accuracy preserved across continuation-mode pairs---suggest that a large component of the depth signal is text-intrinsic rather than tied to a specific generator.

Second, Qwen-rewrite exhibits catastrophic transfer failure.
Classifiers trained on Qwen-rewrite retain only 61--63\% of
within-model accuracy when evaluated on Pythia or OLMo
(45--50\% by $\tau$).
The reverse direction transfers asymmetrically: Pythia/OLMo${\to}$Qwen-rewrite retains 70--72\% of within-model accuracy, higher than the forward 61--63\% but still far below continuation-mode transfer rates (80--92\%).
This confirms that rewrite-mode classifiers rely on generation
artifacts that do not generalize across models, in contrast
to Qwen-continuation, which achieves 80--85\% retention to the same targets.

At the 0v1 boundary, cross-model pairwise $\auc$ exceeds 0.96
for all model pairs, confirming that the human-vs.-synthetic
distinction is consistently transferable across all tested generators
and modes.
The transfer degradation concentrates at deeper boundaries
(1v2 and beyond), where model- and mode-specific factors dominate.

The aggregate picture is one of modest cross-model loss:
mean pairwise $\auc$ is 0.6099 within-model versus 0.5905
cross-model.
This gap is driven primarily by Qwen-rewrite; among
continuation-mode pairs the within/cross difference narrows
further.

%% ====================================================================
\subsection{Feature Degradation Ordering}
\label{sec:feature_degradation}

The transfer results indicate that depth signals are largely text-intrinsic.
We next ask what drives discrimination: if the signal is text-intrinsic, different generators should rely on the same features in the same order.
We test this by computing single-feature $\auc$ rankings
independently for each model and comparing them via rank
correlation.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Top-3 features by single-feature $\auc$ ranking for each
model configuration.
Features shared across all three continuation-mode models are in bold.
Qwen-rewrite's top feature (\texttt{freq\_entropy}) is mode-specific.
Spearman $\rho$ (continuation-mode pairs): Pythia--OLMo 0.95,
Pythia--Qwen-continuation 0.9143, OLMo--Qwen-continuation 0.85.}
\label{tab:top_features}
\begin{tabular}{cllll}
\toprule
Rank & Pythia & OLMo & Qwen-rw & Qwen-cont \\
\midrule
1
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_std}}
  & \texttt{freq\_entropy}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}} \\
2
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d2\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_std}} \\
3
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d2\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d2\_std}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Among continuation-mode models, single-feature $\auc$ rankings
are highly correlated:
Pythia vs.\ OLMo $\rho = 0.95$,
Pythia vs.\ Qwen-continuation $\rho = 0.9143$,
OLMo vs.\ Qwen-continuation $\rho = 0.85$
(all $\rho \geq 0.85$).
The top-3 features---\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}, \texttt{surp\_std},
and \texttt{surp\_d2\_std}---are shared (up to ordering) across
all three continuation-mode configurations
(Table~\ref{tab:top_features}).
All three measure variability of surprisal or its derivatives,
capturing the \emph{heterogeneity} of token-level predictability
across the text.
That these features degrade in a shared order across generators
suggests a common mechanism: each generation step smooths the
token-level surprisal landscape, reducing its variance in a
model-independent fashion.

Qwen-rewrite diverges: its top-ranked feature is
\texttt{freq\_entropy}, a lexical diversity measure absent from
the continuation-mode top-3 for any model.
This corroborates the transfer results in
Section~\ref{sec:transfer}---rewrite-mode classifiers learn
partly from instruction-following artifacts rather than the
shared surprisal-based signals.

Kendall $\tau$ provides a complementary, more conservative
perspective:
Pythia vs.\ OLMo $\tau = 0.733$,
Pythia vs.\ Qwen-continuation $\tau = 0.695$,
OLMo vs.\ Qwen-continuation $\tau = 0.543$.
Cross-mode correlations are lower:
Pythia vs.\ Qwen-rewrite $\tau = 0.467$,
OLMo vs.\ Qwen-rewrite $\tau = 0.429$.

\paragraph{Limitation.}
The high Spearman $\rho$ characterizes the \emph{aggregate}
feature ranking, but at the depth-pair level the agreement
weakens: $\tau \approx 0.37$ at the 1v2 boundary.
This means that while the overall importance ordering is shared,
the relative contribution of individual features at the
discrimination boundary---where precision matters most---varies
across models.
We view this as a genuine limitation of the text-intrinsic
interpretation and a direction for future investigation.

%% ====================================================================
\subsection{Generation Mode Effect}
\label{sec:generation_mode}

Finally, we ask whether generation mode---an experimental design choice rather than a text property---affects depth detectability.
Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct provides a controlled comparison: rewrite (instruction-based paraphrasing) and continuation (prompt truncation) share the same model weights, as defined in Section~\ref{sec:method}, isolating the effect of generation protocol.

Rewrite mode yields higher 1v2 $\auc$ than continuation:
0.6955 vs.\ 0.6112, a difference of $+$8.4 percentage points.
The advantage persists at 2v3
(0.5893 vs.\ 0.5609, $\Delta = +$2.8\,pp)
and narrows at 3v4
(0.5435 vs.\ 0.5409, $\Delta = +$0.3\,pp),
with both modes converging toward chance at deeper levels.
The amplified detectability under rewrite mode is consistent
with instruction-following introducing systematic deviations
from the source text's style---additional artifacts that are
discriminable but mode-specific rather than text-intrinsic.

Transfer between modes is asymmetric.
A classifier trained on Qwen-continuation and evaluated on Qwen-rewrite
retains 89\% of within-model accuracy
(0.3440 vs.\ 0.3875 diagonal),
whereas the reverse direction---Qwen-rewrite trained,
Qwen-continuation tested---retains 82\%
(0.3466 vs.\ 0.4229 diagonal).
The direction of the asymmetry is intuitive:
continuation-mode signals form a subset of the information
available in rewrite-mode data
(which adds instruction-following artifacts on top),
so a continuation-trained classifier can partially recognize
rewrite-mode outputs but not vice versa.

This asymmetry is mirrored in the feature rankings.
Qwen-rewrite's top feature (\texttt{freq\_entropy}) is
mode-specific and ranks outside the top-3 for every
continuation-mode model.
Qwen-continuation's top feature (\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}) is shared
with Pythia and OLMo, confirming that continuation mode
captures primarily text-intrinsic depth signals.

The practical implication is a detectability--generalizability
tradeoff.
Rewrite-mode classifiers achieve higher absolute $\auc$ but
transfer poorly across models
(Qwen-rewrite$\to$Pythia/OLMo: 61--63\% retention).
Continuation-mode classifiers sacrifice 8.4\,pp of within-model
$\auc$ but achieve robust cross-model transfer
(Qwen-continuation$\to$Pythia: 84--85\%).
For deployment scenarios requiring model-agnostic depth
estimation, continuation-mode features provide a more reliable
foundation despite lower raw discriminability.

%% ====================================================================
\subsection{Representation Dependence of $\Kempirical$}
\label{sec:neural_probe}

The preceding sections establish $\Kempirical = 2$ using a 15-dimensional hand-crafted feature set.
A natural question is whether this boundary reflects a fundamental limit of the generational depth signal or an information bottleneck imposed by projecting high-dimensional text representations into 15 statistical summaries.
To disentangle these possibilities, we replace the hand-crafted features with frozen LLM hidden states and train a lightweight MLP probe on the same classification task.

\paragraph{Setup.}
We extract last-layer hidden states from a frozen Qwen2.5-1.5B model (\texttt{float16}), apply attention-masked average pooling to obtain 1536-dimensional document embeddings, and train a two-hidden-layer MLP ($1536 \to 512 \to 256 \to 6$, ReLU, dropout 0.1) with 5-fold GroupKFold cross-validation on the Qwen-continuation dataset (Table~\ref{tab:s7_neural_probe}).
The probe's limited capacity ensures that any discriminability reflects depth information already encoded in the frozen representations rather than patterns learned de novo.
% TODO(exp-015-rerun): Pythia/OLMo neural probe setup details here

\paragraph{Results.}
% TODO(exp-015-rerun): cross-model neural probe comparison table
Preliminary results on the Qwen-continuation dataset are reported below; cross-model validation on Pythia and OLMo is pending.
The neural probe achieves 6-class accuracy of 0.4335 (vs.\ 0.3875 for LightGBM with 15D features).
The pairwise $\auc$ profile reveals a shifted discrimination boundary:
\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lccccc}
\toprule
 & 0v1 & 1v2 & 2v3 & 3v4 & 4v5 \\
\midrule
15D (LightGBM)   & 0.997 & 0.611 & 0.561 & 0.541 & 0.514 \\
Neural (MLP)      & 0.987 & 0.698 & 0.620 & 0.593 & 0.575 \\
$\Delta$\,(pp)    & $-$1.0 & $+$8.7 & $+$5.9 & $+$5.2 & $+$6.1 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The neural probe's 2v3 $\auc = 0.6195$ ($\text{std} = 0.0094$ across folds) exceeds $\theta = 0.60$, yielding $\Kempirical^{\text{neural}} = 3$---one discriminable boundary beyond what the 15D feature set recovers on the same data.
The 15D classifier on the same dataset gives 2v3 $\auc = 0.5609$ (Section~\ref{sec:kstar_boundary}), well below $\theta$.
The improvement concentrates at the 1v2 and 2v3 boundaries ($+$8.7 and $+$5.9\,pp, respectively), where the 15D features lose most of their discriminative power; at the already-trivial 0v1 boundary the neural probe is marginally \emph{lower} ($-$1.0\,pp), consistent with both representations saturating the human--synthetic gap.
At 3v4, the neural probe reaches $\auc = 0.5930$---below $\theta$ but closer to the threshold than any 15D configuration---hinting that a still richer representation might push the boundary further.

\paragraph{Interpretation: $\Kstar$ hierarchy.}
These preliminary results motivate a three-level hierarchy of discrimination boundaries:
\[
  \Ktheory \;\geq\; \Kempirical^{\text{neural}} \;\geq\; \Kempirical^{\text{15D}}
\]
where $\Kempirical^{\text{15D}} = 2$ is the operationally deployable boundary measured with model-free, interpretable features, and $\Kempirical^{\text{neural}} = 3$ is a representation-dependent ceiling accessible only through model-specific probing.
The gap between the two confirms that the 15D feature set does not saturate the available depth signal: at least one additional discriminable generation boundary exists in the frozen representations but is lost during projection into the hand-crafted feature space.
The theoretical upper bound $\Ktheory$---the boundary achievable with an optimal representation and classifier---remains unknown but is at least~3.

\paragraph{Interpretability--discriminability tradeoff.}
The two $\Kempirical$ estimates serve complementary purposes.
The 15D boundary ($\Kempirical = 2$) is model-free, interpretable, and computationally lightweight: features are extracted from surface-level token statistics without access to model internals, and the LightGBM classifier trains in seconds.
This makes it suitable for deployment in data curation pipelines.
The neural boundary ($\Kempirical^{\text{neural}} = 3$) requires a frozen copy of a specific LLM for embedding extraction, is opaque in the features it exploits, and incurs $100\times$+ computational overhead for inference.
It is valuable as a theoretical exploration tool---demonstrating that deeper depth signals \emph{exist}---but impractical for the model-agnostic deployment scenarios where depth estimation is most needed.
Notably, the neural probe's advantage does not alter the headline result for practitioners: $\Kempirical = 2$ remains the relevant boundary for deployable depth estimation with current feature technology.

\paragraph{Caveats.}
The 2v3 boundary under neural probing is marginal: the mean $\auc$ of 0.6195 exceeds $\theta = 0.60$ by only $+$1.95\,pp, and individual fold variation (std $= 0.0094$) places this margin within approximately two standard deviations of the threshold.
These results should be treated as preliminary evidence that the 15D boundary is representation-dependent, not as a firm revision of $\Kempirical$.
% TODO(exp-015-rerun): Pythia/OLMo K*(neural) results here
% TODO(exp-015-rerun): bootstrap CIs for neural probe pairwise AUC
% TODO(exp-015-rerun): cross-model neural probe comparison table
Critically, the current neural probe data covers only the Qwen-continuation dataset; cross-model validation on Pythia and OLMo is pending.
Until confirmed across model families, $\Kempirical^{\text{neural}} = 3$ should be interpreted as a single-dataset preliminary finding rather than a general result.
